title: The Biggest Barrier to Better EFB Software Isn't the Software — It's Running the Program
summary: Jeppesen ForeFlight and Stratix's Manage My EFB DaaS launch exposes an underappreciated truth: for many airlines, the deployment and device-management burden is a bigger obstacle to EFB adoption than anything the software itself is missing.
body_markdown:
Jeppesen ForeFlight and Stratix launched Manage My EFB in June — a Device-as-a-Service bundle that wraps ForeFlight's EFB platform, Apple iPad hardware, lifecycle services, and connectivity into a single per-device monthly subscription. The announcement was relatively quiet, which is a shame, because the model it describes points at something the flight-ops-tech industry doesn't talk about honestly enough: the software is rarely the hard part of an EFB program. The deployment, device management, refresh cycles, and compliance overhead are.

## The Adoption Problem Nobody Puts on a Press Release

Anyone who has spent time on the delivery side of aviation technology deals knows that the signed contract is often the easy milestone. What comes after — staging devices, managing configurations across bases, handling OS updates that break something on a carefully approved software stack, keeping hardware current without triggering a re-approval cycle — that's where EFB programs quietly stall. Airlines run into this whether they're deploying across a 50-aircraft regional fleet or a 400-aircraft mainline operation. The scale changes, but the underlying friction doesn't.

Manage My EFB's DaaS model bundles all of that into one subscription. <cite index="28-4">The offering introduces a new, subscription-based delivery model that combines devices, Jeppesen ForeFlight EFB software, Stratix lifecycle services, and connectivity into a single, predictable cost per device per month.</cite> That's a meaningful structural change in how airlines absorb a flight-deck software program, not just a pricing convenience. It converts capital expenditure and internal IT burden into a managed operating cost — which, in an industry where finance teams and ops teams often have very different tolerance for complexity, actually matters.

What makes this particularly worth noting is where the friction has historically lived. It's rarely been about ForeFlight's feature set. The platform covers flight planning, charts, weather, checklists, and briefing workflows with enough depth that most commercial operators aren't sitting around wishing it did more. <cite index="28-6">The solution is designed to scale from regional operators to global carriers, supporting both commercial and business aviation customers.</cite> The question for most airlines considering a ForeFlight-based EFB program has been operational: who owns the devices, who handles replacements, who manages MDM, who manages the update cycle. Stratix takes that question off the table.

## Why the Industry Underestimates the Cockpit Side

I recently polled industry professionals on where AI will have the biggest safety impact in aviation. The results were revealing: 52% said maintenance and anomaly detection, 17% said ATC flow and conflict management, 17% said preflight planning and briefing — and only 14% picked cockpit decision support. That number has stuck with me. It's not that the 14% are wrong about maintenance AI's importance; the data case for predictive maintenance is genuinely strong. But the cockpit-decision and preflight-briefing categories, taken together, represent the intelligence layer that pilots actually interact with on every single flight. The relative underestimation of that layer is real, and I think it partly reflects the same pattern that shows up in EFB adoption: there's more glamour in the AI story than in the deployment story, and the deployment story is what determines whether any of that AI actually reaches the flightdeck.

The DaaS model is one way to close that gap. By removing the internal-IT and capital-allocation hurdle, it lowers the activation energy for carriers that want to modernize their EFB program but don't have the organizational bandwidth to run a device fleet alongside everything else. <cite index="23-7,23-8">Jeppesen ForeFlight has built the platform around the kinds of data pilots and operators rely on — flight-planning data, operational records, and aviation regulations — rather than broad general-purpose AI.</cite> Getting that onto the flightdeck reliably, at scale, is the harder problem than building it.

## The Model Has Limits Worth Acknowledging

This isn't a perfect solution for every operator. <cite index="1-4">Fleets that require heavy enterprise control over installed configurations and automated device provisioning may find that ForeFlight's governance surface isn't oriented around deep EFB-as-a-managed-endpoint workflows.</cite> Carriers with large, complex IT organizations and existing MDM infrastructure may find the Stratix layer redundant rather than additive. The model probably fits best at the mid-market — regional carriers, charter operators, and business aviation flight departments that lack dedicated IT teams but are large enough to have real EFB compliance obligations.

But even where it's not a perfect fit, it's asking the right question. The conversation in this industry spends a lot of time on what EFB platforms can do — AI-assisted briefing, dynamic checklists, weather data architecture — and not nearly enough on the operational model that gets those capabilities into pilots' hands consistently and at fleet scale. That's the real constraint, and it deserves more direct attention than it usually gets.
